screens.title: Upgradeable Contracts (Proxies)
screens.narratorSegment: Blockchain immutability is a core guarantee: deployed bytecode does not change. That guarantee creates a real engineering problem when you discover bugs or need new features. Upgradeable contracts solve this by separating identity from logic. In the proxy pattern, users keep interacting with a fixed-address proxy that stores state, while the proxy delegates logic calls to replaceable implementation contracts. This lets you deploy new logic without migrating user data or changing the contract address. In this lesson we will study the two dominant proxy patterns — Transparent and UUPS — learn how initializer functions replace constructors for upgradeable contracts, and walk through a Hardhat + OpenZeppelin Upgrades deployment example. You will also see the practical risks to manage: storage layout, centralization of upgrade keys, and upgrade-time bugs. By the end, you will understand why upgradeability is powerful but must be treated as an explicit design choice with clear security controls. Consider this: what policy will your team use to authorize upgrades?

Each objective ties to a competency milestone so you can verify you can deploy, inspect proxy and implementation addresses, and reason about storage layout. Think of these objectives as both conceptual and hands-on: you'll learn definitions and run the deployment flow end-to-end.

screens.title: The immutability problem
screens.narratorSegment: Immutability means that once smart contract bytecode is on-chain, its code does not change. That property gives users strong guarantees: transactions will always be executed by the same code. But immutability also creates a fundamental operational challenge. If you discover a logic bug, or want to ship new features, redeploying a new contract typically means a new address and separate storage. Users' balances, approvals, and application state remain locked in the old address unless you build migrations — a costly and error-prone process. Upgradeable contracts solve this practical problem by separating address from logic. The core definition we use is: an upgradeable contract design preserves an address and storage while allowing the logic at that address to change by delegating execution to replaceable implementations. A concrete example: a token contract deployed at address A that accumulates user balances; if you redeploy token logic at address B then you either have to move every balance to B or ask users to migrate. That user friction is often unacceptable. A common misconception is to assume constructors will initialize proxy state — they do not. Constructors run for implementation deployments, not proxy initialization. Key takeaway: immutability protects users but requires design patterns to enable safe evolution.

keyIdea.title: Why it matters
keyIdea.text: Immutability prevents in-place fixes; upgradeability gives teams a controlled way to change behavior while keeping user state intact.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Immutability
The immutability problem
Why deployed contracts cannot be changed and why that can be a problem.
Definition

Immutability: deployed bytecode does not change. This guarantees predictability but prevents in-place fixes.

Concrete example
A token at address A holds user balances. Redeploying logic to address B requires moving or migrating balances — costly for users.
Common misconception: "Constructors initialize proxy state." Not true — constructors run during implementation deployment and do not populate proxy storage.
Why this matters
  • Users expect continuity: addresses used in UIs and approvals should keep working.
  • Migrations are fragile: moving state invites errors and user drop-off.
  • Upgradeability resolves these by separating identity (proxy) from logic (implementation).
Key Takeaway

Use upgradeable patterns when you need evolution without data migration; but plan governance and storage safety from the start.

screens.title: Proxy and Implementation roles
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding roles is essential to design and debug upgradeable systems. The proxy contract is the permanent on-chain identity: users call the proxy address, which contains the persistent storage used by the application. The proxy contains minimal logic to forward or delegate execution to an implementation contract. Delegatecall is the crucial low-level primitive: it executes implementation code in the context of the proxy's storage, so state variables live at the proxy address. The implementation contract contains business logic and can be replaced by deploying a new implementation and updating the proxy's reference. A concrete example: if a proxy stores a mapping of balances, the implementation's functions reading or writing balances will, when called via delegatecall, access the proxy's storage slots. A common mistake is changing the order or types of state variables in a new implementation. That causes storage collision: the same storage slots now represent different variables, corrupting state. In short, the proxy holds state and identity; implementations hold logic. Designing implementations to be storage-layout-stable and using OpenZeppelin's storage checks reduces the risk. Reflect: when you inspect a transaction, check which address's storage changed to understand where the state lives.

keyIdea.title: Storage separation
keyIdea.text: Proxy stores the state. Implementation holds logic and runs with the proxy's storage via delegatecall.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Proxy Architecture
Proxy and Implementation roles
How a proxy dispatches calls and where state lives.
Architecture overview
Proxy (fixed address) — stores state, delegates calls
Implementation (replaceable) — contains logic
Delegatecall executes implementation code with the proxy's storage context. That is why state persists across upgrades.
Example: a balances mapping in the proxy remains intact after switching implementations because reads and writes target the proxy's storage slots via delegatecall.
Storage collision risk
  • Adding or reordering state variables in a new implementation changes slot assignments.
  • Different types or inherited storage can shift subsequent slots.
  • OpenZeppelin's upgrades plugins perform layout checks to catch many unsafe changes.
Common mistake

Changing the order of state variables in a new implementation can corrupt user balances or mappings. Always maintain stable storage layout or use reserved slots.

screens.title: Transparent Proxy Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: The Transparent Proxy Pattern resolves a practical conflict: what if the implementation and the proxy both define a function with the same name, for example an administrative function? Transparent proxies solve this by distinguishing callers: if the caller is the admin or owner, calls that match proxy management functions are handled by the proxy itself; regular users' calls are forwarded to the implementation. This design avoids function selector clashes between the proxy and implementation. A concrete example is a proxy that exposes an upgrade function only callable by the admin. If a user accidentally calls that selector, the proxy routes it safely. Transparent proxies are easy to reason about because the upgrade logic sits in the proxy and is always under admin control. The trade-off is slightly higher gas because the proxy contains additional control logic and checks for admin calls. A common misconception is to assume transparent proxies make the implementation immutable — they do not. You can still upgrade the implementation; the proxy simply makes sure admin actions are enforced and does not delegate admin selectors to implementations. Key takeaway: Transparent proxies centralize upgrade logic in the proxy to prevent selector clashes but incur extra proxy-side control logic.

keyIdea.title: Transparent pattern
keyIdea.text: Proxy distinguishes admin calls from user calls, preventing function selector clashes by keeping upgrade logic in the proxy.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Transparent Proxy
Transparent Proxy Pattern
Owner/admin separation of upgrade functions to avoid name clashes.
How it works
  1. Proxy checks caller identity.
  2. If caller is admin, handle admin functions within proxy.
  3. Otherwise delegatecall to implementation.
This avoids function selector collisions between proxy and logic contracts.
Concrete example & trade-offs
Example: admin calls upgrade function on proxy; proxy runs upgrade logic directly rather than delegating.
Trade-offs: simpler admin model but extra gas and a larger proxy surface. Upgrades remain possible and must be governed carefully.
Misconception: Transparent proxies do not eliminate upgrade risk; they only organize where upgrade logic lives.

screens.title: UUPS Proxy Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: UUPS, the Universal Upgradeable Proxy Standard, shifts upgrade responsibilities into the implementation contract. The proxy remains minimal — it simply holds a reference to the implementation and forwards calls. The implementation includes explicit upgrade functions like _authorizeUpgrade and _upgradeTo, and it executes the logic to change the implementation pointer. This reduces proxy size and gas costs for interactions, because the proxy no longer performs admin checks for each call. A concrete example: when using OpenZeppelin's UUPS helpers, your implementation implements an _authorizeUpgrade function that checks permissions, for example requiring onlyOwner or a multisig. A key advantage is gas efficiency and leaner proxy code. The critical risk is that the implementation itself must correctly preserve upgrade hooks. If a future implementation accidentally removes or mis-implements _authorizeUpgrade, upgrades can be lost or made unsafe. A common misconception is that UUPS is automatically safer — it is not; it simply changes where the upgrade control lives. Key takeaway: UUPS is recommended by OpenZeppelin for many projects because of gas savings, but it demands disciplined implementation and careful upgrade testing. UUPS Proxy Pattern means upgrade logic lives in implementation, making proxies leaner but requiring careful implementation-side upgrade controls.. In practical terms, upgrade logic in the implementation for gas efficiency and control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › UUPS Proxy
UUPS Proxy Pattern
Upgrade logic in the implementation for gas efficiency and control.
How it works
  • Proxy stores implementation pointer and delegates calls.
  • Implementation exposes _authorizeUpgrade and _upgradeTo.
  • Upgrade is triggered by implementation code that modifies the proxy pointer.
Example & risk
Example: implementation includes _authorizeUpgrade guarded by onlyOwner or a multisig check.
Risk: a future implementation that removes authorization hooks can make upgrades unsafe or permanently disable upgradeability. Careful audits and tests are essential.

screens.title: Initializable and initializer functions
screens.narratorSegment: Constructors run when an implementation contract is deployed, not when a proxy points to it. For upgradeable logic that runs via delegatecall, constructors do not initialize the proxy's storage. OpenZeppelin provides Initializable as a base pattern: replace constructors with initialize functions marked by an initializer modifier. The initializer ensures the function runs at most once when called through the proxy. Additionally, implementations often include a constructor that calls _disableInitializers to prevent direct initialization of the implementation contract itself, which could be a security risk. A concrete example: when writing an ERC20 upgradeable token, you call ERC20_init(name, symbol) inside initialize, then _mint the initial supply. If you forget to call these init functions for inherited components, inherited state may remain uninitialized and functions may fail or behave incorrectly. A common misconception is thinking the implementation's constructor will set up inherited initial state — it will not for proxy-based usage. Key takeaway: always use Initializable patterns and call all relevant __init helpers for each inherited upgradeable base contract to ensure consistent state in the proxy. Initializable and initializer functions means use initializer functions and _disableinitializers to safely set up proxy storage, and call all inherited __init helpers.. In practical terms, replacing constructors safely in upgradeable contracts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Initializable
Initializable and initializer functions
Replacing constructors safely in upgradeable contracts.
Pattern summary
Implement initialize functions with the initializer modifier. Use __Base_init helpers for inherited contracts. Include a constructor that calls _disableInitializers in the implementation to prevent direct initialization.
// Example initialize
function initialize(string memory name, string memory symbol) initializer public {
  __ERC20_init(name, symbol);
  _mint(msg.sender, initialSupply);
}
Common mistakes
  • Forgetting to call inherited __init helpers.
  • Leaving implementation initializers enabled, allowing someone to initialize the implementation directly.
Tip: include _disableInitializers in the constructor of the implementation to block direct initialization attempts.

screens.title: UpgradeableToken.sol explained
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a compact upgradeable ERC20 implementation to reinforce the initializer pattern and constructor safety. The implementation inherits Initializable and ERC20Upgradeable. The constructor includes a call to _disableInitializers to prevent the implementation from being initialized directly. The initialize function is marked initializer and calls ERC20_init to initialize inherited state, then mints an initial supply into the proxy's storage. This is crucial: state changes during initialize operate against the proxy storage because initialize is called through the proxy during deployProxy. The contract also shows a newFeature function to illustrate adding functionality in a later implementation. A concrete example: after deploying the proxy and initial implementation, calling name() through the proxy returns the token name stored in proxy storage. A typical misconception is to assume constructor initialization will flow to the proxy — it does not. Always call inherited init routines. For upgrades, add functions in a new implementation and redeploy, making sure you preserve storage layout. When reading code, focus on where storage is set, what modifiers guard upgrades, and whether disableInitializers protects the implementation contract. Takeaway: follow the Initializable conventions and verify inherited initializers are invoked.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › UpgradeableToken.sol
UpgradeableToken.sol explained
A step-through of an upgradeable ERC20 using Initializable.
Key code excerpt
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

import "@openzeppelin/contracts-upgradeable/token/ERC20/ERC20Upgradeable.sol";
import "@openzeppelin/contracts-upgradeable/proxy/utils/Initializable.sol";

contract UpgradeableToken is Initializable, ERC20Upgradeable {
    /// @custom:oz-upgrades-unsafe-allow constructor
    constructor() {
        _disableInitializers();
    }

    function initialize(string memory name, string memory symbol, uint256 initialSupply) initializer public {
        __ERC20_init(name, symbol);
        _mint(msg.sender, initialSupply);
    }

    function newFeature() public pure returns (string memory) {
        return "This is a new feature!";
    }
}
Annotations
constructor: calls _disableInitializers to protect implementation.
initialize: marked initializer and calls __ERC20_init to initialize inherited pieces.
newFeature: shows how adding logic happens in an implementation update.
Key Takeaway

Always call __init for inherited upgradeable contracts and protect implementations from direct initialization.

screens.title: Deploying with Hardhat and OpenZeppelin Upgrades
screens.narratorSegment: Deploying an upgradeable contract with Hardhat and OpenZeppelin Upgrades follows a clear sequence. First, install the plugin and upgradeable contracts package. Second, require the plugin in your hardhat. config so the upgrades A P I becomes available. Third, prepare your contract to be upgradeable — inherit Initializable and use initialize functions. Fourth, write a deployment script that calls upgrades. deployProxy with kind: 'uups' and passes initializer name. The deployProxy helper deploys both the implementation and the proxy, calls initialize via the proxy so proxy storage is populated, and returns an ethers contract instance that's connected to the proxy address. A concrete example is the provided deploy script which logs the proxy, implementation, and admin addresses, then demonstrates reading the token name and a balance. A common pitfall is forgetting to pass the initializer function name or arguments, which can leave the proxy uninitialized. After deployment, verify implementation and admin addresses using upgrades. erc1967 helpers. Key takeaway: deployProxy bundles deployment, linking, and initialization so that proxy storage is correctly set at creation time. Confirm addresses and test basic reads and writes through the proxy to validate the deployment.

const { ethers, upgrades } = require("hardhat");

const UpgradeableToken = await ethers.getContractFactory("UpgradeableToken");

screens.title: Upgrade lifecycle and verification
screens.narratorSegment: Upgrading an implementation is a careful, multi-step lifecycle: design, test, deploy the new implementation, perform storage-layout checks, then execute the upgrade through the authorized flow. With UUPS, the implementation exposes upgrade functions and typically checks authorization in _authorizeUpgrade. The actual upgrade involves deploying the new implementation contract and invoking the upgrade routine so the proxy points to the new implementation. Afterward, verify that state variables retain expected values by calling read-only functions via the proxy. A common concrete sequence: deploy new implementation, call the implementation's upgrade entry that your admin is allowed to call, then confirm balances and mappings are intact through the proxy. Use upgrades. erc1967 helper functions to log the new implementation address and admin address. A common pitfall is skipping storage layout checks — reordering variables in the new implementation can silently corrupt state. Always run OpenZeppelin's storage layout comparisons and unit tests that assert invariant state across upgrades. Key takeaway: upgrades are a deployment activity plus a governance decision — test, verify, and document every step. Upgrade lifecycle and verification
How to perform an upgrade and confirm state preservation.
Upgrade steps

  2. Run storage layout checks against the previous implementation.
  3. Deploy new implementation contract.
  4. Execute upgrade via authorized call (UUPS: call implementation upgrade function).

Skipping storage layout checks or insufficient tests can silently corrupt critical state after an upgrade.

screens.title: Security risks and trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Upgradeability introduces powerful capabilities and several critical risks you must manage. First, centralization risk: the party holding the upgrade key can change logic and potentially introduce malicious code or backdoors. Mitigate this with multisig wallets, governance proposals, and time locks. Second, upgrade bugs: a flawed implementation can break core functionality; therefore, upgrades require thorough testing and audits. Third, storage collisions: changing variable order or types in a new implementation can corrupt data stored in the proxy; use automated storage layout checks and reserved storage slots to avoid this. Fourth, reentrancy and new vulnerabilities can be introduced during upgrades; include regression tests and reentrancy guards. Finally, added complexity increases the audit surface and developer cognitive load. A common misconception is to assume upgrades reduce security concerns because you can patch quickly. In reality, upgrades increase the need for process discipline. Concrete mitigation steps: require multisig+timelock for upgrades, run OpenZeppelin layout checks, write migration and regression tests that assert invariants, and have a rollback plan. Key takeaway: treat upgradeability as a governance and engineering process rather than a feature to be used casually.

Centralization, upgrade bugs, storage collisions, and complexity.
Centralization Risk
The upgrade key holder can change the implementation. Use multisig, governance, and timelocks to reduce risk.
Storage Collisions
Adding or reordering state variables can corrupt storage. Run layout checks and reserve storage slots to avoid collisions.
Upgrade Bugs & Complexity

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the most important concepts to remember. Immutability means deployed code does not change, which motivates upgradeable patterns when you need to fix bugs or add features. A proxy contract provides a stable address and storage, delegating execution to implementation contracts that contain logic. Transparent proxies keep upgrade logic in the proxy and separate admin calls from user calls to avoid function selector clashes. UUPS proxies move upgrade logic into the implementation to reduce proxy size and gas at the cost of relying on correctly implemented upgrade hooks. Initializable replaces constructors in upgradeable contracts; always call inherited __init functions and disable initializers in implementations. Finally, upgradeability introduces governance and security responsibilities: manage upgrade keys, run storage layout checks, and maintain thorough testing and audit practices. Keep these core ideas in mind when designing production upgradeable systems.

fullNarratorScript:
Blockchain immutability is a core guarantee: deployed bytecode does not change. That guarantee creates a real engineering problem when you discover bugs or need new features. Upgradeable contracts solve this by separating identity from logic. In the proxy pattern, users keep interacting with a fixed-address proxy that stores state, while the proxy delegates logic calls to replaceable implementation contracts. This lets you deploy new logic without migrating user data or changing the contract address. In this lesson we will study the two dominant proxy patterns — Transparent and UUPS — learn how initializer functions replace constructors for upgradeable contracts, and walk through a Hardhat + OpenZeppelin Upgrades deployment example. You will also see the practical risks to manage: storage layout, centralization of upgrade keys, and upgrade-time bugs. By the end, you will understand why upgradeability is powerful but must be treated as an explicit design choice with clear security controls. Consider this: what policy will your team use to authorize upgrades?

These objectives map to practical skills you will practice. First, you will clearly explain the immutability problem and why upgradeable contracts exist. That means understanding that deployed bytecode cannot be changed and recognizing the user-experience and migration costs of redeployment. Second, you will differentiate proxy patterns: you should be able to list the behavioral difference between Transparent proxies and UUPS proxies, and explain when one might be preferred. Third, you will describe the distinct roles of proxy contracts and implementation contracts, including where state lives and how delegation preserves addresses. Finally, you will be introduced to OpenZeppelin Upgrades Plugins and the developer workflow to deploy upgradeable contracts with Hardhat. Each objective ties to a competency milestone so you can verify you can deploy, inspect proxy and implementation addresses, and reason about storage layout. Think of these objectives as both conceptual and hands-on: you'll learn definitions and run the deployment flow end-to-end.

These practical objectives emphasize hands-on deployment and security reasoning. You will prepare upgradeable contracts by inheriting OpenZeppelin's Initializable patterns and replacing constructors with initialize functions. You will write and run a deploy script that uses upgrades. deployProxy to create a UUPS proxy and confirm the implementation and admin addresses with upgrade helpers. You will perform a simple upgrade, observe storage persistence, and recognize storage collision signals. Finally, you will evaluate security trade-offs: identify who holds the upgrade key, design multisig or governance protections, and run storage-layout checks. Each skill is measurable: run the sample UpgradeableNFT deployment, mint an asset through the proxy, then deploy a patched implementation that adds a new feature. These exercises build both technical and governance muscles, helping you balance flexibility with safety in production systems. Learning Objectives — Practical Skills means prepare, deploy, and reason about upgrades; test that state persists and storage layout remains safe after changes.. In practical terms, hands-on outcomes and security awareness you will demonstrate. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Immutability means that once smart contract bytecode is on-chain, its code does not change. That property gives users strong guarantees: transactions will always be executed by the same code. But immutability also creates a fundamental operational challenge. If you discover a logic bug, or want to ship new features, redeploying a new contract typically means a new address and separate storage. Users' balances, approvals, and application state remain locked in the old address unless you build migrations — a costly and error-prone process. Upgradeable contracts solve this practical problem by separating address from logic. The core definition we use is: an upgradeable contract design preserves an address and storage while allowing the logic at that address to change by delegating execution to replaceable implementations. A concrete example: a token contract deployed at address A that accumulates user balances; if you redeploy token logic at address B then you either have to move every balance to B or ask users to migrate. That user friction is often unacceptable. A common misconception is to assume constructors will initialize proxy state — they do not. Constructors run for implementation deployments, not proxy initialization. Key takeaway: immutability protects users but requires design patterns to enable safe evolution.

Understanding roles is essential to design and debug upgradeable systems. The proxy contract is the permanent on-chain identity: users call the proxy address, which contains the persistent storage used by the application. The proxy contains minimal logic to forward or delegate execution to an implementation contract. Delegatecall is the crucial low-level primitive: it executes implementation code in the context of the proxy's storage, so state variables live at the proxy address. The implementation contract contains business logic and can be replaced by deploying a new implementation and updating the proxy's reference. A concrete example: if a proxy stores a mapping of balances, the implementation's functions reading or writing balances will, when called via delegatecall, access the proxy's storage slots. A common mistake is changing the order or types of state variables in a new implementation. That causes storage collision: the same storage slots now represent different variables, corrupting state. In short, the proxy holds state and identity; implementations hold logic. Designing implementations to be storage-layout-stable and using OpenZeppelin's storage checks reduces the risk. Reflect: when you inspect a transaction, check which address's storage changed to understand where the state lives.

The Transparent Proxy Pattern resolves a practical conflict: what if the implementation and the proxy both define a function with the same name, for example an administrative function? Transparent proxies solve this by distinguishing callers: if the caller is the admin or owner, calls that match proxy management functions are handled by the proxy itself; regular users' calls are forwarded to the implementation. This design avoids function selector clashes between the proxy and implementation. A concrete example is a proxy that exposes an upgrade function only callable by the admin. If a user accidentally calls that selector, the proxy routes it safely. Transparent proxies are easy to reason about because the upgrade logic sits in the proxy and is always under admin control. The trade-off is slightly higher gas because the proxy contains additional control logic and checks for admin calls. A common misconception is to assume transparent proxies make the implementation immutable — they do not. You can still upgrade the implementation; the proxy simply makes sure admin actions are enforced and does not delegate admin selectors to implementations. Key takeaway: Transparent proxies centralize upgrade logic in the proxy to prevent selector clashes but incur extra proxy-side control logic.

UUPS, the Universal Upgradeable Proxy Standard, shifts upgrade responsibilities into the implementation contract. The proxy remains minimal — it simply holds a reference to the implementation and forwards calls. The implementation includes explicit upgrade functions like _authorizeUpgrade and _upgradeTo, and it executes the logic to change the implementation pointer. This reduces proxy size and gas costs for interactions, because the proxy no longer performs admin checks for each call. A concrete example: when using OpenZeppelin's UUPS helpers, your implementation implements an _authorizeUpgrade function that checks permissions, for example requiring onlyOwner or a multisig. A key advantage is gas efficiency and leaner proxy code. The critical risk is that the implementation itself must correctly preserve upgrade hooks. If a future implementation accidentally removes or mis-implements _authorizeUpgrade, upgrades can be lost or made unsafe. A common misconception is that UUPS is automatically safer — it is not; it simply changes where the upgrade control lives. Key takeaway: UUPS is recommended by OpenZeppelin for many projects because of gas savings, but it demands disciplined implementation and careful upgrade testing. UUPS Proxy Pattern means upgrade logic lives in implementation, making proxies leaner but requiring careful implementation-side upgrade controls.. In practical terms, upgrade logic in the implementation for gas efficiency and control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Constructors run when an implementation contract is deployed, not when a proxy points to it. For upgradeable logic that runs via delegatecall, constructors do not initialize the proxy's storage. OpenZeppelin provides Initializable as a base pattern: replace constructors with initialize functions marked by an initializer modifier. The initializer ensures the function runs at most once when called through the proxy. Additionally, implementations often include a constructor that calls _disableInitializers to prevent direct initialization of the implementation contract itself, which could be a security risk. A concrete example: when writing an ERC20 upgradeable token, you call ERC20_init(name, symbol) inside initialize, then _mint the initial supply. Upgradeability introduces powerful capabilities and several critical risks you must manage. First, centralization risk: the party holding the upgrade key can change logic and potentially introduce malicious code or backdoors. Mitigate this with multisig wallets, governance proposals, and time locks. Second, upgrade bugs: a flawed implementation can break core functionality; therefore, upgrades require thorough testing and audits. Third, storage collisions: changing variable order or types in a new implementation can corrupt data stored in the proxy; use automated storage layout checks and reserved storage slots to avoid this. Fourth, reentrancy and new vulnerabilities can be introduced during upgrades; include regression tests and reentrancy guards. Finally, added complexity increases the audit surface and developer cognitive load. A common misconception is to assume upgrades reduce security concerns because you can patch quickly. In reality, upgrades increase the need for process discipline. Concrete mitigation steps: require multisig+timelock for upgrades, run OpenZeppelin layout checks, write migration and regression tests that assert invariants, and have a rollback plan. Key takeaway: treat upgradeability as a governance and engineering process rather than a feature to be used casually.

Let's summarize the most important concepts to remember. Immutability means deployed code does not change, which motivates upgradeable patterns when you need to fix bugs or add features. A proxy contract provides a stable address and storage, delegating execution to implementation contracts that contain logic. Transparent proxies keep upgrade logic in the proxy and separate admin calls from user calls to avoid function selector clashes. UUPS proxies move upgrade logic into the implementation to reduce proxy size and gas at the cost of relying on correctly implemented upgrade hooks. Initializable replaces constructors in upgradeable contracts; always call inherited __init functions and disable initializers in implementations. Finally, upgradeability introduces governance and security responsibilities: manage upgrade keys, run storage layout checks, and maintain thorough testing and audit practices. Keep these core ideas in mind when designing production upgradeable systems.

Use these three compact reminders as a checklist during development and deployment. First, always treat constructors and initializers differently: constructors run on the implementation, while initializers must be called through the proxy to set proxy storage. Second, validate storage layout on every change: OpenZeppelin's tooling will help, but you should include unit tests that assert critical invariants across upgrades. Third, enforce upgrade governance: hold upgrade power in multisig or DAOs, add timelocks, and require audits for any implementation change. Keep these three checks in your deployment pipeline and you will reduce the most common and severe upgrade risks when running upgradeable contracts in production.
